Yesterday’s cliffhanger

The robot pollinator you debated is already a practical idea

What changed
They are not mechanical bees

The deployed systems replace one action — vibration or airflow at the flower. The strongest case is indoors, where pollination is already a managed input.

Revisit position · 90 sec

Does that detail move your position from yesterday? Which assumption changed?

Most people move once they hear indoors. Yesterday’s debate assumed a machine replacing wild pollinators in a field; the real product replaces a person with a vibrating wand in a greenhouse. The ethics of the second are not the ethics of the first.

Commercial examples: Arugga Polly+; Polybee greenhouse drones.

Greenhouse pollination

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B02 / 40

The framing

A plant cannot run, hide, or call for help

1
It cannot move

Drought, pests, pathogens and neighbours arrive. The plant must tolerate them.

2
It signals slowly

Stress appears as chemistry, heat and colour, often before visible damage.

3
It stays put

The same individual can be measured repeatedly, from the same place.

4
So sensing is the point

AI can monitor continuously and act before the damage is obvious.

Immobility is a vulnerability for the plant and an enormous advantage for the sensor.

Four things to take away

CATCHEarly detection can be worth more than late accuracy
ASKWho can afford the tools, who owns the data, and who is left out

The lecture moves from perception → action → timing → governance.

Sensing

Turning a field into a data stream.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B05 / 40

The scales of sensing

Four altitudes, four different decisions

1
Satellite · region

Fields to countries every few days. Coarse pixels, huge coverage.

2
Drone · field

Centimetre detail on demand, weather permitting.

3
Machine · row

Cameras on sprayers or robots see every plant at working speed.

4
Ground · plant

Phones, fixed cameras and soil probes watch one root zone closely.

The right altitude is set by the decision, not by the technology.

“Irrigate zone 4 tomorrow” and “spray this weed now” are different sensing problems.

Seeing beyond the eye

Plants show stress in light we cannot see

Visible

Human inspection.

NIR

Leaf structure signal.

Index

Combine bands.

Map

Where stress is emerging.

The information was physically present before the human could see it.

The same conceptual move as Herculaneum: new sensing exposes a hidden trace, then AI interprets it.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B07 / 40

Plant disease from a photograph

99% in the lab can become 31% in the field

99.35%

same-condition test accuracy

31.4%

different-condition accuracy

54,306 leaf images, and both numbers reported in the same paper.

The number everyone quotes is only meaningful if the test world matches the deployment world. Mohanty, Hughes & Salathé, Frontiers in Plant Science, 2016.

PlantVillage

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B08 / 40

Diagnose the failure

Why 99% becomes 31%

1
Detached leaf

Training images isolate one leaf on a plain background.

2
One problem

Real plants can have multiple diseases, or nutrient stress that mimics one.

3
Shortcuts

A model can learn the photography setup instead of the disease.

4
Closed labels

A field contains “unknown” cases the training taxonomy never saw.

3 questions · 2 min

You are handed a crop model with 97% test accuracy. What three questions do you ask before letting it advise a farmer?

How were the images collected? What happens on a class it has never seen? Was it tested at a different site or in a different season? Any model that cannot answer the third has reported a number about its training conditions, not about your farm.
AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B09 / 40

What good looks like

Field-ready models are evaluated differently, not trained longer

Random split

  • Train and test drawn from the same pool
  • Every site appears on both sides
  • The model is tested on ground it has seen
  • A number that flatters the model

Site split

  • Whole sites held out of training
  • The test site is genuinely new ground
  • Harder number, honest number
  • The change costs nothing to make

Also add an “unknown / refer to expert” option. A field tool should be allowed to abstain.

Acting

When a prediction becomes a nozzle, a laser, a gripper or a pollinator.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B11 / 40

Targeted spraying

See & Spray: the same field, a fraction of the chemical

>5M

acres of reported use in 2025

≈50%

average reduction in non-residual herbicide

See → decide → act → result: cameras scan the ground, the model separates crop from weed, and individual nozzles fire.

About 31 million gallons of spray mix saved. Read manufacturer numbers as claims with a very large field sample, not as an independent randomized trial.

See & Spray

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B12 / 40

Why it matters

A perception problem with a chemistry-sized payoff

Environment

Less herbicide entering soil and water; less selection pressure for resistance.

Economics

Input cost can fall dramatically when every square metre is not treated.

Real-time AI

The deadline is milliseconds: identify a weed and trigger hardware while moving.

The catch

Expensive equipment means the gains may arrive first on farms with capital.

In physical AI, latency can bind before accuracy does.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B13 / 40

Beyond spraying

Once perception works, the end effector is an engineering choice

01
Laser weeding

Computer vision identifies weeds; lasers kill them without herbicide.

02
Mechanical thinning

Remove surplus seedlings with plant-by-plant precision.

03
Selective harvest

Judge ripeness and pick only what is ready.

04
Variable-rate inputs

Water and fertilizer by zone rather than uniformly.

Example: Carbon Robotics LaserWeeder — onboard computer vision plus lasers for chemical-free weed control.

Laser weeding

03

Pollination

Replacing one action that an insect performs.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B15 / 40

The problem

Why build a pollinator at all?

01
Pollinator pressure

Wild and managed pollinators face habitat loss, pesticides, pathogens and climate stress.

02
Greenhouses

Enclosed environments and artificial light can make bee management difficult.

03
Some crops need vibration

Tomato flowers release pollen when vibrated — a task a bee or a person can perform.

04
Labour

Hand pollination is skilled, repetitive, time-sensitive work.

Notice the strongest case is indoors, where there was never a wild pollinator to displace.

Pollination

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B16 / 40

What exists

Three approaches, and none is a mechanical bee

Deployed
Air-pulse robots

Ground robots use computer vision to find receptive flowers and deliver calibrated air pulses.

Deployed
Micro-drones

Small drones use their downwash to move pollen, and collect crop imagery while flying.

Research
Insect-scale platforms

Tiny fliers and sticky-gel concepts are impressive research, not routine field tools.

Commercial greenhouse examples: Arugga Polly+ and Polybee.

Deployed systems

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B17 / 40

The AI inside it

The hard part is knowing which flower, and when

Find

The flower among leaves.

Judge

Whether it is at a receptive stage.

Aim

Position the effector accurately.

Record

Log each treatment.

A bee solves all four with no external map. The robot gets something the bee never produced: a per-flower record of the crop.

Automation can create data as a by-product of action — and that by-product may end up worth more than the pollination.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B18 / 40

Structured disagreement

Substitution, or a reason not to fix the problem?

The case for

  • Indoors it replaces labour, not a wild ecosystem
  • Reduces dependence on shipped bee colonies
  • Works on demand, at night, in winter
  • Produces crop data while acting

The case against complacency

  • Pollination is only one ecosystem service
  • A substitute can weaken habitat arguments
  • Outdoor field-scale pollination remains far harder
  • A free ecosystem service becomes a purchased input
Argue the other side · 4 min

In pairs, argue the side you disagree with. Then write one sentence you both accept.

The sentences that survive usually sound like: “A greenhouse substitute is defensible; treating it as a reason to stop protecting wild pollinators is not.” Forcing students onto the opposite side produces better sentences than open debate.

04

Early detection

Finding it before it becomes a permanent problem.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B20 / 40

Why timing dominates

The invasion curve: cost rises, options disappear

Stage 1
Absent

Prevention. Cheapest of all, and invisible — nobody gets credit for an invasion that never happened.

Stage 2
Arrived, few

Eradication still possible. This is the window where detection changes the outcome.

Stage 3
Established

Containment only. Cost climbs steeply and the goal shifts to slowing the spread.

Stage 4
Widespread

Permanent management. The species is now part of the landscape and the budget.

A 70% detector at stage 2 can be worth more than a 99% detector at stage 4.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B21 / 40

Detection route 1

Environmental DNA: find a species you never see

Sample

Water, soil or air.

Sequence

Shed DNA fragments.

Match

Against a reference library.

Flag

Likely presence.

Good at rare, cryptic, nocturnal or aquatic species at low density.

Open question: a DNA signal can travel. When is a detection actionable?

eDNA sampling

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B22 / 40

Detection route 2 · Citizen science

Millions of people already carry a species detector

Phone + model + community
How it works

A person photographs a plant or insect, a model proposes an identification, and experts or the community confirm or correct it.

Why it matters
Coverage no agency could fund

Every record carries a location, a date, and a photograph attached for verification.

The model does not need to be right every time. It needs to surface the right photographs to an expert.

Citizen science

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B23 / 40

Detection route 3 · Remote sensing

Watching the landscape change from orbit

Spectral signature

Leaf chemistry can make some invasive plants stand out from native vegetation.

Timing as a clue

Different green-up or flowering dates can separate species that look alike.

Predict spread

Climate, terrain, roads and trade routes help forecast where to search next.

Best practice combines routes: satellites narrow the search; people and eDNA confirm it.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B24 / 40

The false-alarm problem

Setting the alarm threshold is a policy decision

Miss a real invasion

  • The eradication window closes
  • Cost compounds for years
  • The failure stays invisible until late
  • Nobody can point to the moment it was missed

Raise a false alarm

  • Crews and budget are spent
  • Growers may face unnecessary disruption
  • Trust in the system can erode
  • The failure is immediate and visible
Set threshold · 3 min

Your model outputs P(invasion). Where do you set the alarm — and who should make that call: the modeller, the agency, or the growers?

Whoever sets it is deciding whose costs count. By default it is the modeller, who bears none of them. That is the argument for making the threshold an explicit, published, revisable policy rather than a constant buried in code.
AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B25 / 40

Inside the farm gate

The same logic applies to crop disease

01
Before symptoms

Spectral and thermal signals can precede visible damage.

02
Spore / air sampling

Airborne spores or DNA can flag arrival before a field outbreak.

03
Forecasting

Weather models predict when infection pressure becomes high.

04
Why it pays

Early action needs less chemical and protects more yield.

The invasion curve applies at every scale — continent, country, farm, single greenhouse bay.

05

Systems

The greenhouse as a closed-loop AI system.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B27 / 40

Controlled environments

When you control light, water, heat and air, growing becomes control

Sense

Climate and crop.

Predict

Response to settings.

Optimize

Yield against energy and water.

Act

Lighting, heat, irrigation.

A greenhouse makes the whole loop observable: the system can act, measure the consequence, and update.

Competitions have tested autonomous control against experienced growers on real crops.

Controlled environment

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B28 / 40

Limits of the loop

Why the field is not a bigger greenhouse

Inside

  • Most variables are measured
  • Many variables are controllable
  • Cycles repeat
  • Failures are contained

Outside

  • Weather is an input, not a setting
  • Soil and pests vary spatially
  • Every season shifts the distribution
  • A wrong decision can play out for months

Controlled environments are where closed-loop AI matures fastest. Open fields are where most food is grown.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B29 / 40

Breeding and genetics

A search problem with a one-season evaluation step

Phenotyping

Automated imaging measures height, canopy, leaf area and stress across thousands of plants.

Genomic prediction

Models estimate which genetic crosses are worth testing in the field.

Climate matching

Predict which varieties suit conditions a region has not experienced before.

AI matters most when evaluation is slow or expensive: it helps decide which candidates deserve a season of testing.

06

Who benefits?

The questions that outlast the technology.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B31 / 40

Question 1 · Access

The technology arrives where the capital already is

1
Cost floor

Sensor-equipped machines are expensive. The savings are real and the entry ticket is high.

2
Scale mismatch

Most farms globally are small; tools built for uniform mega-fields may fit poorly.

3
Connectivity

Cloud-dependent tools assume reliable rural broadband.

4
What could close it

Phones, cooperatives, shared machinery, public mapping and open models.

A technology can be efficient and still widen inequality if access is uneven.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B32 / 40

Question 2 · Data

Who owns what a machine learns about a farm?

What is collected

  • Yield and moisture at metre scale
  • Machine telemetry
  • Multi-year field history
  • Imagery of every plant

Why it is contested

  • Aggregated data has market value
  • Vendors can create lock-in
  • Farm data improves a model sold back to farmers
  • Repair and portability rights are unresolved
Take a position · 3 min

Should the data belong to the farm, the machine owner, the platform, or everyone who helped generate it?

Every answer has a cost, and naming yours is the exercise. Farm ownership fragments the dataset that makes the model good. Platform ownership creates lock-in. A public pool raises the question of who pays to maintain it — and who is trusted to hold it.
AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B33 / 40

Question 3 · Ecosystem

Optimizing a field is not caring for a landscape

What gets measured

  • Yield
  • Cost
  • Input use
  • Machine hours

What often does not

  • Soil biology
  • Pollinator habitat
  • Water downstream
  • Birds in the hedgerow

An optimizer protects what is in its objective. Unmeasured goods are not protected by good intentions.

The same failure as the risk algorithm that predicted cost and called it health.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B34 / 40

Question 4 · Labour

Automation arrives fastest where labour is hardest to find

The pull

  • Seasonal labour shortages
  • Physically punishing work
  • Timing is unforgiving
  • Machines can work at night

The consequence

  • Whole communities depend on farm work
  • Displacement is concentrated
  • New jobs need different training
  • Who gets those jobs is a policy choice

“Labour-saving” describes the machine. It does not describe the social outcome.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B35 / 40

A caution

On “plant intelligence”: be careful with the word

Well established
Plants sense and respond

Light, gravity, touch, chemistry and damage. They signal internally and respond adaptively.

Genuinely contested
The vocabulary

Whether “memory,” “learning,” “decision” or “intelligence” are the right words is debated among plant scientists.

The discipline
Say what was measured

“Growth changed after repeated stimulation” is a finding. “The plant remembered” is an interpretation.

Plants remain remarkable whether or not we use cognitive vocabulary.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B36 / 40

Putting it together

Design a surveillance programme

Brief — a new tree-killing pest is 300 km away. You have one season and a modest budget.

Decide 1
Where to look

What data predicts likely arrival points?

Decide 2
Who looks

Satellite, traps, eDNA, field crews, or the public?

Decide 3
Threshold

What probability triggers an alarm?

Decide 4
Authority

Who gets to set that threshold?

Groups of four · 7 min

Report out: which stage of the invasion curve are you betting on?

The professional answer layers the methods: broad cheap coverage to narrow the search, expensive confirmation only on hits. A programme that spends its whole budget on one high-accuracy method has bet everything on looking in the right place.
AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B37 / 40

Two lectures together

What changed when we moved from animals to plants?

Animals + swarms

  • Biology gave us algorithms
  • Sensing finds things that move and hide
  • Ethical question: watching
  • Coordination without a leader

Plants + agriculture

  • Biology is the managed system
  • Sensing monitors things that stay put
  • Ethical question: ownership and access
  • Optimization with an explicit objective

Both lectures rest on one idea: cheap sensing plus inference makes previously invisible signals actionable.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B38 / 40

The course-level synthesis

Six lectures, one recurring pattern

Measure

An instrument exposes a trace.

Represent

Turn the trace into data.

Learn

Extract a pattern too complex for hand-written rules.

Decide

A human owns the consequence.

Carbonized scrolls · protein structures · chest radiographs · whale codas · a leaf with a lesion.

Different sciences. Same pipeline. The last step never became automatic.

AI × Nature · Plants · Lecture 6B39 / 40

Takeaway

The field was always sending signals

We finally built something that reads them.

01 · TIMINGFor invasions and outbreaks, an early rough answer can beat a late precise one
02 · GENERALIZATION99% in the lab and 31% in the field can come from the same model
03 · OBJECTIVESAn optimizer protects only what is written into its objective
Exit ticket · 2 min

Name one thing a farm optimizer would not measure. Write the objective term you would add to protect it — and say who pays.

The “who pays” clause is what separates a wish from a policy. Soil biology, pollinator habitat and downstream water all have plausible objective terms; none has an obvious payer, which is precisely why they go unmeasured.

Sources: Mohanty et al. (2016); John Deere See & Spray; Carbon Robotics; Arugga and Polybee; eDNA and remote-sensing literature; autonomous greenhouse work.
